articles.title: Black Friday, EU summit disarray, and Centre Party support for Kristersson
articles.heading: Nordic Alert
articles.fulltext:
Global key stories
The US stock market was closed yesterday while European stocks continued to rise (Euro Stoxx 50 +2%) amid the recovery in the IT sector. The euro weakened somewhat at yesterday's close. US stock futures are pointing upward ahead of Black Friday's short trading, which could be a test to see if the recovery continues. Asian stock markets are trading upward this Friday morning. Oil prices are heading for their first weekly rise in four weeks, as escalating fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen, as well as ongoing attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, raise concerns about global energy supply. Yesterday,
 two Italians were killed
 in an Iranian drone strike on Kuwait. The victims were technicians employed at the Italian subsidiary of the German arms company Rheinmetall and worked at an air defense station in Kuwait.
Economic statistics.
 Today, preliminary inflation data for France and Spain, French household expenditures, German unemployment, inflation expectations within the euro area, as well as trade balance and retail inventories in the USA, are published. 
Pablo Hernández de Cos will become the new head of the ECB central bank
, after the leaders of the euro countries backed him at the summit in Brussels yesterday. According to 
the FT 
, France and Germany reached an agreement earlier this month regarding the three highest positions within the ECB. As part of this agreement, Frenchwoman Laurence Boone will replace Isabel Schnabel on the ECB's Executive Board, where she will be responsible for market operations, while German Markus Brunnermeier will take over from ECB chief economist Philip Lane. De Cos will take office in February 2027. 
Snubs all around at the EU summit.
 The specially convened summit to achieve a breakthrough regarding the EU's next budget ended in chaos after the leaders, divided into opposing camps, refused to give up their principles and openly 
questioned 
whether an agreement could be reached before the end of the year. Formally, they have one year left to decide on the EU budget for 2028–2034, but many hope to have it ready soon before France's presidential election in April next year, where the far-right politician Marine Le Pen could become the new president. 
Updated credit ratings are expected later today for France (S&P), Hungary (S&P), and South Africa (S&P and Moody's). This weekend there are general elections in Spain and local elections in Taiwan.
Worth reading from SEB
: 
Norwegian GDP
 for the third quarter and 
SEB FI & FX Strategy
Nordic key stories
The krona strengthened yesterday and the OMX30 index rose 2%.
Swedish politics.
 After an extraordinary meeting yesterday, the Centre Party leadership decided it will support for Ulf Kristersson (M) as prime minister. On Sunday, the Centre Party leadership is expected to present its decision to the council of trust ("förtroenderådet"), where they will make the decisive decision on whether the party will vote for Kristersson as prime minister, according to 
SVT
. However, it is unclear whether everyone in the parliamentary group is willing to vote yes in the prime minister vote on Monday. Today is also the last day for parliamentary parties to submit their own budget motions ahead of the 2027 state budget. Since the current government is a caretaker government and submitted a caretaker budget on November 12, several parties have announced their own alternatives.
During the day, the National Institute of Economic Research's business barometer, GDP for the third quarter, and the trade balance will be released. 
In Norway, statistics on unemployment and retail trade are also released.

articles.title: Black Friday, snöpligt slut på EU-toppmöte och C-stöd för Kristersson
articles.heading: Morning Alert
articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
Börsen i USA var stängd under gårdagen medan europeiska aktier fortsatte uppåt (Euro Stoxx 50 +2%) i samband med återhämtningen inom IT-sektorn. Euron försvagades något vid gårdagens slut. Aktieterminerna i USA pekar uppåt inför Black Fridays korta handel som kan bli ett test för att se om återhämtningen håller i sig. Börserna i Asien handlas uppåt nu på fredagsmorgonen. Oljepriserna är på väg mot sin första veckouppgång på fyra veckor, då de eskalerande stridigheterna mellan Saudiarabien och huthierna i Jemen samt de fortsatta attackerna mot fartyg i Hormuzsundet väcker oro över den globala energiförsörjningen. Igår dödades
 två italienare
 i en iransk drönarattack mot Kuwait. Offren var tekniker anställda vid tyska vapenföretaget Rheinmetalls italienska dotterbolag och arbetade vid en luftförsvarsstation i Kuwait.
Ekonomisk statistik.
 Idag publiceras preliminära inflationsdata för Frankrike och Spanien, franska hushållsutgifter, tysk arbetslöshet, inflationsförväntningar inom euroområdet samt handelsbalans och detaljhandelns lager i USA. I Norge släpps också statistik på arbetslöshet och detaljhandel. 
Pablo Hernández de Cos blir ny chef för centralbanken ECB
, efter att euroländernas ledare ställde sig bakom honom på toppmötet i Bryssel igår. Enligt 
FT 
ska Frankrike och Tyskland tidigare denna månad ha nått en överenskommelse rörande de tre högsta posterna inom ECB. Som en del av denna överenskommelse kommer franska Laurence Boone att ersätta Isabel Schnabel i ECB:s direktion, där hon kommer att ansvara för marknadsoperationerna medan tyske Markus Brunnermeier kommer att ta över efter ECB:s chefsekonom Philip Lane. De Cos tillträder i februari 2027. 
Snöpligt slut på EU-toppmöte.
 Det särskilt sammankallade toppmötet för att nå ett genombrott i fråga om EU:s nästa budget slutade i kaos efter att ledarna, uppdelade i motstående läger, vägrade att ge avkall på sina principer och öppet 
ifrågasatte 
om en överenskommelse skulle kunna nås innan årets slut. Formellt har man ett år kvar att bestämma EU-budgeten för 2028–2034 men många hoppas få den klar i närtid före Frankrikes presidentval i april nästa år, där den högerextrema politikern Marine Le Pen kan bli ny president. 
Uppdaterade kreditvärderingsbetyg väntas senare idag för Frankrike (S&P), Ungern (S&P) och Sydafrika (S&P och Moody’s). I helgen är det allmänna val i Spanien och lokalval i Taiwan.
Läsvärt från SEB
: 
Norsk BNP
 för tredje kvartalet och 
SEB FI & FX Strategy
Sverige
Kronan stärktes under gårdagen OMX30-index steg 2%.
Svensk politik.
 Efter ett extrainsatt möte igår beslutade Centerpartiets ledning att man ska rösta för Ulf Kristersson (M) till statsminister. På söndag väntas C-ledningen lägga fram sitt beslut för förtroenderådet där man kommer att fatta det avgörande beslutet om partiet ska rösta för Kristersson som statsminister, enligt 
SVT
. Det är dock oklart om alla i riksdagsgruppen kan tänka sig att rösta ja vid statsministeromröstningen på måndag. Idag är också sista dagen för riksdagspartierna att lämna in egna budgetmotioner inför statsbudgeten för 2027. Eftersom den nuvarande regeringen är en övergångsregering, och lämnade en övergångsbudget den 12 november, har flera partier aviserat egna alternativ.

articles.title: France: Fiscal adjustment or escalating confrontation?
articles.heading: SEB FI & FX Strategy
articles.fulltext:
At a glance: 
In market focus.
 AI trade; Fed; growth vs inflation; Middle East & oil; stock market positioning (short).
Global macro and risk appetite.
 Tech stocks have sold off heavily since the start of October on concerns about the duration of the massive investment boom. A series of outages and data leaks has sown doubts about security in an AI world, adding to fears of a political backlash against unregulated AI. Although IT suppliers to the AI boom delivered strong Q3 reports, the hyperscalers building the datacentres did not surprise to the upside and appear to have lost earnings momentum. Meanwhile, the Fed, or at least Governor Waller, has turned more hawkish, and hawkish signals are now reflected in tighter financial conditions. Combined with the slowdown in datacentre capex, this means we likely have to go through a tactical downturn in the economy. Without a more supportive Fed, that downturn risks becoming deeper. However, markets have now priced a significant slowdown in the AI investment boom, suggesting a near-term trough for tech stocks and a rally for the broader market is likely if the Fed turns more accommodating.
US macro: Mixed start to Q4 after very strong Q3.
 Surging consumption and strong AI investments boosted GDP growth in Q3, according to the revised data. Flat household spending in October supports our expectations of a slowdown in Q4, however. Inflation has picked up during the fall, with relatively broad increases in both goods and services. PPI indicates upside risks in the near term, while the decline in energy prices is a downside risk further on.
USD short rates: Hawkish Fed challenged by shaky equity markets. 
Fed members signal strong support for a December hike, and we expect members to forecast at least one more hike in 2027 at the December meeting. A couple of Fed members, including Governor Waller, are talking about 50bp hikes, while others are discussing hikes at consecutive meetings. Falling equity prices may, however, force the Fed to proceed more cautiously, in a situation in which it has highlighted equity wealth as a supportive factor for consumer spending. We now expect the Fed to hike in December and March. Forwards price in around 65bp of hikes until summer 2027, which we see as fair in the current situation. 
USD bonds: Twisty road ahead. 
The bond rally since mid-November has been fuelled by the equity sell-off, perceived risks of overtightening and lower inflation expectations. A stabilisation in risk appetite could send yields higher again, while continued risk-off would support bonds. The 10Y yield may have seen its cycle peak, but we are hesitant to bet on a sustained downtrend until closer to the policy rate peak.
France: Fiscal adjustment or escalating confrontation?
 We outline four scenarios for France over the next 12 months. Our most likely scenario is prolonged fiscal drift, where a crisis is avoided, and the OAT-Bund spread fluctuates mainly in a 130-170bp range. However, there is a significant risk of escalating fiscal confrontation, and a major market test may not come until after the 2027 presidential election. 
Spain: Snap election – a solution to the parliamentary deadlock? 
Spain will hold a snap election on 29 November. Opinion polls point to a change of government, which would inherit a relatively favourable economic backdrop and a declining public debt-to-GDP ratio. The main risk is difficulty in passing budgets and reforms, rather than an immediate deterioration in public finances. 
Read more here
.
EUR short rates: Hawkish ECB tone since the October meeting has hardened further.
 Recent comments have been mainly hawkish, highlighting risks of indirect and second-round effects, as well as resilient growth. The GC is aligned for a December hike, with some members saying market pricing for 2027 (35bp on top of 25bp in December) looks reasonable, while some remain more cautious.
EUR bonds: Time for a rebound in yields? 
The German 10Y yield has declined even more than its US counterpart over the past two weeks. The ECB policy rate trajectory discounted by markets has softened to a level we regard as fair (55-60bp of hikes in total). We think risks have shifted towards the 10Y Bund yield rebounding back to our 3.30-3.50% target range. A continued equity sell-off is the key risk to this view.
EUR/USD: The outlook is murky. 
 EUR/USD has moved lower with the 10Y rate differential. Safe-haven demand and steady foreign inflows into US assets have outweighed our starting hypothesis that an AI-bubble unwind would weigh on the USD. The outlook is murky. The most probable scenario is likely a Hormuz deal, which, combined with very long USD positioning and a pause in France's deterioration, leaves room for EUR/USD to move higher into Q1. We would then expect a setback in H2 2027 as France's issues return. Positive news from France alongside a Hormuz deal would extend the move higher. Escalation around Hormuz together with renewed problems in France would push EUR/USD lower. Given the uncertainty, our bias would be towards expressing views through options.
 We go through this in more detail in next week's FX Pilot.

macro
,

France: Fiscal adjustment or escalating confrontation? 
France’s fiscal challenges are likely to remain a source of volatility for European bond markets over the coming year. Our base-case scenario is neither a decisive resolution nor full-blown crisis, but prolonged fiscal drift: enough political compromise to preserve market access, yet insufficient adjustment to stabilise public debt. However, we see a significant risk that confrontation over fiscal policy escalates, with consequences extending far beyond French government bonds.
Over the coming 12 months, periods of relative calm may allow French government yield spreads to tighten relative to Germany without resolving the underlying fiscal problem. A more durable recovery in confidence requires a credible change in policy direction, which would also facilitate activation of the ECB’s Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), if deemed necessary, to curb unwarranted market movements. Italy’s past experience offers some useful lessons about how that change can emerge, and how markets may respond before debt dynamics visibly improve.
Lessons from Italy: Credibility can precede improvement in debt metrics.
 Italy’s bond-market turbulence in 2018-19 illustrates how fiscal confrontation can undermine confidence, but also how a policy compromise can restore it. Spending plans, euroscepticism and a budget dispute with Brussels pushed the Italian 10Y yield spread vs Germany above 300bp. Pressure subsequently eased as the government moderated its deficit target and reached a compromise with the EU. Fiscal concessions and ECB monetary easing supported a further narrowing in yield spreads in 2019. Notably, markets recovered as greater confidence in the direction of policy helped to bring borrowing costs down relative to Germany while the long-term fiscal challenge prevailed.
In 2022, the energy shock and the withdrawal of ECB net bond purchases exposed Italy’s sensitivity to higher financing costs. The 10Y Italian-German yield spread approached 250bp in June, while Mario Draghi’s resignation as Italy’s prime minister in July added to political uncertainty. Flexible reinvestment of the ECB’s bond portfolio and the announcement of its Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) helped contain the risk of excessively fragmentation. The incoming Meloni government’s fiscal restraint subsequently reinforced market confidence and facilitated tightening of Italian and other spreads. 
iBoxx sector spreads vs. Euribor 6M swaps & 10Y sovereign spreads vs. Germany
Four scenarios for France. 
We present four stylised scenarios over the next 12 months. The probabilities are our judgemental assessments. In aggregate, we assign a 55% probability to outcomes that avoid acute fiscal confrontation and a 45% probability to scenarios in which confrontation escalates. All spread levels below refer to 10Y government yield spreads.
Credible consolidation: 15%.
 A credible political agreement establishes a deliverable medium-term fiscal adjustment. Provided implementation reinforces investor confidence, the French-German yield spread could move back towards 80-90bp. The essential ingredient is not simply an agreement, but confidence that the adjustment can be carried through.
Prolonged fiscal drift: 40%. 
This is our most likely individual scenario. Sufficient political compromise preserves market access and avoids an immediate escalating crisis, but fiscal adjustment falls short of stabilising debt. As political and market stress subsides, the spread settles around 130-170bp, potentially interrupted by recurring bouts of widening to higher levels. This would represent an uneasy stabilisation rather than a long-term solution with France remaining vulnerable beyond the 12-month scenario horizon. 
 Market-forced reset: 25%. 
Mounting market pressure becomes the catalyst for a credible fiscal response. The 10Y spread initially widens above 250bp, before retracing as investors gain confidence in the adjustment. The defining feature is that policymakers respond relatively quickly, likely after the presidential election. As Italy’s experience demonstrates, a credible change in direction can restore confidence before actual debt metrics improve.
Prolonged confrontation: 20%. 
Policymakers resist adjustment, allowing sovereign stress and its wider effects to intensify. The spread would remain above 250bp for longer, with a risk of materially higher levels. Spillovers into bank funding and other euro-area markets would become more persistent. Stabilisation would require an eventual change in fiscal direction, potentially alongside conditional European support to France and the ECB’s additional support for the banking system via targeted long-term refinancing operations. 
See 
Euro area fragmentation risk: How will the ECB respond?
, 16 October, for our thoughts of the ECB’s likely response sequence. 
Broader market implications. 
France-related uncertainty remains a key source of potential market turbulence for broader markets through the April/May 2027 presidential election, while implications differ considerably between scenarios.
Under our base scenario of prolonged fiscal drift, highly rated non-French public-sector borrowers, including agencies, regional governments and supranationals, could remain relatively resilient vs Euribor swaps. They could nevertheless widen vs their underlying domestic government curves due to safe-haven demand, particularly for Bunds but also other fiscally strong euro area governments.
In case of escalating fiscal confrontation, German government bonds would richen significantly relative to Euribor swaps, particularly at shorter maturities, with a broad-based widening of credit spreads vs swaps. 
The more adverse scenario would be prolonged fiscal confrontation. Rising compensation for liquidity and risk would then be likely to push public-sector bond spreads wider more broadly, particularly if stress became systemic.
The distinction is therefore between recurring volatility that leaves stronger issuers relatively resilient vs swaps and an escalation that produces persistent spillovers across European fixed income. We are preparing for renewed turbulence in the coming months, while recognising that a major test may not come until the second half of 2027, after the French presidential election.

articles.title: Core inflation expected to rise slightly in November
articles.heading: Swedish inflation
articles.fulltext:
CPIF ex energy
 is predicted to rise slightly to 0.3% y/y in November (October 0.1% y/y, Riksbank forecast: 0.9% y/y). Inflation metrics are still heavily dampened by temporary fiscal measures.
CPIF ex energy
corrected for political measures 
(lower VAT and the increased subsidy for public transport) is expected to rise to 1.3% y/y (October 1.1% y/y, Riksbank forecast 1.9% y/y).
CPIF 
is expected to increase to 2.0% y/y (October 1.5% y/y Riksbank: 1.7% y/y) on the back of higher electricity prices. Electricity prices will add 1.3ppt to the month-on-month rate, while fuel prices will decline 0.3ppt. 
Slightly higher core inflation in November 
CPIF excluding energy has been significantly lower than expected for 3-months in a row.
There are still no clear signs of indirect effects from high energy prices, but producer prices on consumer goods have increased slightly on the back of a weaker krona. Pricing plans in the NIER survey remain largely stable. Rising electronics prices, driven by strong AI-related demand, continue to be an upside risk but so far, lower prices on other goods have offset most of the upside pressure. 
Service inflation has declined to very low levels, partly because of a continued reversal of high prices on tourist services during the summer. Prices on package holidays declined markedly in October and we predict prices to fall further November in line with the normal seasonal pattern. We continue to predict service inflation to turn higher, partly due to base effects.
Sharply higher prices on electricity but lower fuel prices in November
Electricity prices are set to rise sharply in November and the contribution to the month-on-month change for CPI is estimated to be 1.3p. The government will repay approximately 30% of the higher electricity prices in November to the households, but in line with similar supports in 2022, 2023 and 2026, this will not affect CPI. Futures imply that electricity prices will decline going forward, and the summer contracts are as much as 75% lower than the price level in November. 
Fuel prices have declined significantly and will lower CPI by 0.3pp. However, fuel prices will rise equally much in December, when the temporary tax reduction on fuels is reversed. The near-term forecast for fuel prices has been lowered significantly in line with the decline in global market prices.
Policy implications
The Riksbank was more hawkish than we expected in September, but we interpreted the message in November as somewhat softer. Governor Thedeén acknowledged that the rate path from September indicated a very low probability for a December hike. Significantly lower inflation supports our view that the probability for a December hike is low, and we stick to our forecast for a second hike in March. The Board continues to warn for second-round effects and deputy Governor Per Jansson does not seem to rule out another rate hike already in December.

articles.title: Nominal bond issuance to increase further in coming years
articles.heading: The SNDO borrowing report
articles.fulltext:
Key points
The NDO kept nominal bond issuance unchanged at SEK 240bn in 2027 and forecast 264bn in 2028, which was higher than we had expected. Issuance volume will be unchanged at SEK 5bn per weekly auction in 2027 and increased to SEK 6bn in 2028.
The forecasts of the underlying budget balance and borrowing requirements were broadly in line with our projections, implying that the maintained high volumes in nominal SGBs are due to a replacement of FX bond issuance.
The NDO lowered the forecast for own FX bonds issuance to zero both 2027 and 2027 (from SEK 19bn per year). This is explained by a request from the Riksbank to borrow SEK 200bn in foreign currency for the Riksbank’s currency reserve. The NDO has not included the re-lending in its forecast, awaiting a formal decision.
Unchanged nominal bond issuance in 2027, further increase in 2028
The Swedish National Debt Office (NDO) kept nominal bond issuance at 240bn in 2027, forecasting 264 bn in 2028. This is SEK 15bn in 2027 and SEK 54bn in 2028 higher than we expected, although the surprise is mainly due to a replacement of FX bond issuance into nominal SEK bonds. The forecasts of the underlying budget balance and borrowing requirements were broadly in line with our projections.
The NDO lowered the forecast for own FX bonds issuance to zero both 2027 and 2027 (from SEK 19bn per year). This is explained by a request from the Riksbank to borrow SEK 200bn in foreign currency for the Riksbank’s currency reserve. The NDO has not included the re-lending in its forecast but assumes that the need for own FX issuance is no longer needed. The NDO has over the last 2-3 years issued SEK 20-40bn in foreign currency to maintain market presence.
A new 10-year bond will be introduced in the beginning of 2027 by a SEK 20bn syndication (SGB 1069, maturing in February 2038). 
The weekly nominal bond auctions will remain at SEK 5bn and there will be 44 auctions in 2027. Continued deficits and more maturing bonds explain the increase in nominal bond issuance in the coming years. Furthermore, the NDO continues to lower outstanding IL-bonds band which are replaced by nominal bonds but will issue a new IL-bond in 2028 (SGB IL 3117, maturing in 2043). Gross Il-bond issuance is unchanged at SEK 6bn per year in 2027 and 2028.
SGBs are underperforming versus peers following the report, with yields increasing from low levels. The broad outlook remains the same, despite the surprise. Gross issuance is increasing on fiscal policy, defence, infrastructure and Ukraine aid expenditures, but demand has also been robust - so far absorbing the increase in supply, keeping SGB yields at low levels vs swaps and bunds.
The outlook for the budget balance: 
The forecast for the budget balance was largely in line with our forecast. The predicted budget deficit in 2027 was lowered to SEK -173bn (SEB expected SEK -200bn) from SEK -208bn in May, while the budget balance in 2028 is predicted to be SEK -140bn (SEB expected SEK -120bn). 
Re-lending to the Riksbank:
 The Riksbank plans to fund parts of the currency reserve by taking up FX loans via the NDO. If decided, which is highly likely, the Riksbank will request the NDO to borrow foreign currency amounting to SEK 200bn for re-lending. The NDO will wait for a formal request before including the measure in the forecast, but the final impact on the budget balance will most likely be a decrease of SEK 135bn in 2027 and SEK 65bn in 2028. The NDO’s own issuance of FX bonds was reduced to zero already in this report. We had expected the NDO to wait for a formal decision also here. 
Fiscal policy: 
Increasing defence expenditures, transport and increased dental care are the main expenditures, and the NDO continues to assume unfunded fiscal policy measures of SEK 15bn per year in 2027 and 2028. 
The NDO has not considered the measures in the interim budget put forward by the caretaker government on November 12, although this should not affect the budget balance materially given the neutral and stripped-down nature of the interim budget.
Defence and support to Ukraine: 
The government is gradually raising defence spending and has announced a scope for military support to Ukraine amounting to slightly less than 1% of GDP per year in 2026 and 2027. Importantly, on aid to Ukraine, the NDO assumes that total aid will amount to approximately SEK 10 billion per year in 2026-2028. This is SEK 17 billion less per year than in the previous forecast. A large portion of the aid is expected to weigh on the budget balance beyond 2028.

articles.title: Another downside surprise
articles.heading: Norwegian GDP
articles.fulltext:
Mainland GDP growth was once again weaker than expected, rising a minor 0.1% q/q in Q3 while Q2 was also revised lower. Growth has shown an easing trend over the past 1.5 year. Public demand is underpinning growth while private demand is dampened by high costs and interest rates. While growth was weaker than Norges Bank’s 0.3% q/q estimate, employment growth was marginally stronger. Overall, developments should support Norges Bank’s assessment that the output gap is turning slightly negative and reassure the bank that monetary policy is taking effect. This also supports our and the market’s call for an unchanged policy rate in December.
Mainland GDP:
 Sequential growth in mainland GDP surprised on the downside in Q3, rising a minor 0.1% q/q. This was below our, consensus’ and Norges Bank’s 0.3% estimate and growth thus continued to surprise on the downside. At the same time, mainland GDP growth in Q2 was revised 0.2ppt lower to 0.1% while Q1 was lifted by 0.1ppt to 0.3%. Overall, mainland GDP growth has shown a flattening trend this year. Public demand is holding up, supporting activity, while high interest rates are dampening private demand. The composition of growth in Q3 shows that mainland GDP was lifted by a strong rebound in private consumption after two consecutive quarterly declines, while mainland investment was dragged down by a plunge in business investment. Meanwhile, exports of traditional goods contributed positively as imports fell.
This is reflected in production-side data; the vast service sector as well as the public sector contributed positively, output in manufacturing & mining were neutral, while production of other goods was a drag. The latter reflects a 10th consecutive quarterly decline in construction and a fall in volatile sectors, e.g., electricity production and traditional fishing. Volatile sectors lowered mainland GDP with 0.1ppt.
Overall GDP:
 Growth for the overall economy was weaker with total GDP falling 0.3% q/q in Q3, from a downward revised 0.6% q/q in Q2. Production-side data shows that besides a drag from other goods producing sectors, output in the oil sector fell 1.6% q/q, lowering GDP by 0.4ppt. This is mirrored in related demand-side data with oil investment plunging -8.5% q/q. This was partly balanced with a 4.0% q/q upturn in oil & gas exports which resulted in a positive contribution from net trade. Meanwhile, the notoriously volatile inventory component dampened growth in Q3. 
Oil investment:
 Investment plummeted 8.5% q/q in Q3, after broadly stable growth in Q2, and a hefty rise in Q1 of 9.9% q/q. The year-on-year rate thus corrected further down to -12.2%, from previously -3.4%. As most tax subsidized field developments are near completion and the pipeline of new projects is thin, the petroleum cycle is likely to peak this year and turn negative in 2027.
Mainland investment:
 Mainland investments fell 1.8% q/q in Q3. The decline was due to a large fall in business investment (-3.7% q/q), reflecting a significant decline within services extraction and other goods-producing sectors. Public investments (0.3% q/q) offered some support, while a rise in residential investments (0.5% q/q) was not enough to offset the quarterly decline. The latter is still down 20.2% from its peak in Q1 2022. 
Exports of traditional goods:
 Traditional goods export rose 2.3% q/q, driven by strong growth in exports of agriculture, forestry and fishing as well food and beverage while partly offset by a large decline within refined oil products. Meanwhile, imports of traditional goods declined a modest 0.4% q/q. Net trade of traditional goods contributed 0.5ppt to mainland GDP growth. Total exports were stronger, rising 2.7% q/q with a 1.3ppt contribution to total GDP from net trade.
Private consumption:
 Private consumption rose 1.5% q/q, after weakness in H1. Private consumption was revised up 0.1ppt in Q1 while adjusted down 0.2ppt in Q2. In Q3, goods consumption (2.2% q/q) was the main contributor, while service consumption (0.9% q/q) also posted gains. Consumption of other goods (food, clothing and shoes) were particularly strong, while another strong quarter for auto purchases and consumption of electricity also contributed. Growth in services consumption was mainly due to a large increase in accommodation and food service activities, partly due to the strike in the previous quarter and partly due to increased tourism from abroad. 
Employment:
 Employment growth was stable at 0.2% q/q for the fourth consecutive quarter, which continues to run 0.1ppt above Norges Bank’s 0.1% estimate. Growth was mainly due to public sector, rising 0.4% q/q, which accounted for about two-thirds of the increase. Growth in private sector was 0.1% q/q. Growth was strongest in services (0.2% q/q) and retail trade (0.2% q/q), while declining in construction (-0.3% q/q). Number of hours increased 0.1% q/q. Productivity, as measured by mainland GDP per hours worked, rose 0.6% so far this year compared to the corresponding period last year. Note that the figures are preliminary. 
Implications Norges Bank:
 The national accounts data for the third quarter sends mixed signals. On the one hand, mainland GDP growth appears weaker than envisaged which could indicate that the current monetary policy stance is having the desired effect. On the other, the labour market appears somewhat stronger as quarterly employment growth is holding up at 0.2%, and registered unemployment remains marginally below Norges Bank’s trajectory (November data due tomorrow). Overall, developments should support Norges Bank’s assessment that the output gap is turning slightly negative and reassure the bank that monetary policy is taking effect. Norges Bank is balancing the need to bring inflation back to target against the risk of unnecessarily restraining economic activity. Further tightening at this point would raise downside risks to growth, with limited benefits for the long-term inflation outlook. This is already reflected in current market pricing as the likelihood of another rate hike has vanished, and the market now discounts a 25bps cut by September 2027. Final data ahead of the Dec 17th rate decision and MPR are registered unemployment (Nov 27) as well as Nov inflation data and the Regional Network Report (Dec 10).

articles.title: New tariffs, volatile stock markets and strong US macro data
articles.heading: Nordic Alert
articles.fulltext:
Global key stories
Equities fell again yesterday, but a late-day rebound in the US left the closing declines fairly small compared with the intraday lows. The S&P 500 fell 0.3% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq 0.6%, although it was down as much as 4.6% at one point during the day. AI concerns remain the main drag on equities, and Trump again floating the idea of new tariffs (more below) did not help. Uncertainty, and therefore volatility, is clearly elevated right now. However, note that US markets are closed today for Thanksgiving.
Despite the strong macro data during the day (see below), US yields continued to fall. Increased demand for safer government bonds amid the equity turmoil seems a plausible driver. The US dollar also weakened somewhat across the board yesterday. The oil price moved higher for the first time in several days, but at USD 95 per barrel it remains well below early November levels. Asia has followed the late-day recovery in the US, with indices generally higher and the AI-heavy Taiwan index leading at +2.8%. Equity futures also point to a positive start in the US, and an even stronger one in Europe, today.
Tariffs back on the agenda.
 Yesterday, Trump announced a series of new tariffs on 14 countries, including the EU, China, Japan and South Korea, while Norway was spared. Tariffs of up to 20% are proposed for specific product groups, with China and Vietnam facing the highest rates and the EU a proposed 15%. The tariffs will not be implemented immediately, and it is implied that it will take months before they can enter into force.
Higher inflation and growth in the US.
 The Fed's preferred inflation gauge, core PCE, surprised slightly to the upside yesterday, coming in at 3.3% y/y against the expected 3.2% and 3.1% in September. At the same time, the second estimate of Q3 GDP also surprised to the upside, with a strong increase of 4.3% (annualised) versus the expected 3.5%. Growth continued to be driven mainly by strong consumption, but also by increased investment in IT equipment and software, which we regard as a gauge of AI investment. There is therefore reason for some concern going forward if the AI frenzy continues and both these growth drivers take a hit. The slightly higher inflation print, together with stronger growth, strengthens the case for a Fed hike in December and for signalling one or more hikes in its 2027 projections. Note that yesterday, ahead of the data, we added a hike in March to our forecasts – more 
here
.
Today's agenda is relatively light, with the US closed for Thanksgiving.
 We look forward to German consumer confidence, Norwegian Q3 GDP, the Swedish National Debt Office's borrowing report (more below), a speech by the Riksbank's Jansson ("Swedish monetary policy in an uncertain world"), and the start of a two-day Euro summit.
Nordic key stories
Norwegian Q3 GDP today and budget yesterday.
 Mainland GDP rose 0.3% in Q2, while Q1 growth was revised marginally down. This points to lower annual growth this year than previously expected. However, we, the consensus and Norges Bank agree that Q3 will also show growth of 0.3%, with production-side data broadly neutral and demand-side data more mixed. After intensive negotiations, a revised 2027 central government budget proposal was presented yesterday. However, as the Green Party chose to stay outside the agreement, it is not certain that the budget will secure a majority in parliament.
The Swedish National Debt Office publishes its borrowing report today at 09:30.
 We expect the National Debt Office (NDO) to reduce the supply of nominal bond issuance somewhat in 2027 compared with the May plans, and to cut the number of weekly auctions from 48 to 45, implying a total of SEK 225bn in 2027. It will await a formal request from the Riksbank before including increased issuance of foreign-currency bonds in its forecast but is likely to discuss the possible consequences in the report already now. Read more in 
360 Sweden
.
Swedish producer prices rose in October.
 The producer price index (PPI), published yesterday for October, rose 0.9%. This was somewhat of a surprise, as we had expected a 0.2% decline. The increase was partly because electricity prices continued upwards instead of temporarily dropping as we had anticipated. In addition, prices of export goods and consumer goods rose slightly, and we also see that some upward pressure from the exchange rate likely contributed. Regarding electricity prices, we again note sharp increases ahead of the weekend, and November as a whole will contribute strongly to upward pressure on coming PPI releases.

articles.title: Nya tullar, volatila börser och stark makrodata i USA
articles.heading: Morning Alert
articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
Börserna föll igen under gårdagen men framför allt i USA så vände det något på slutet vilket resulterade i tämligen små fall i förhållande till när det var som värst under dagen. S&P 500 föll 0,3% och tekniktunga Nasdaq med 0,6% men var som mest ner runt 4,6% under dagen. Det är främst AI-oron som fortsätter tynga börserna men att Trump återigen vädrade tankar om nya tullar (mer nedan) hjälpte heller inte till. Helt klart är i alla fall att osäkerheten och därmed volatiliteten är stor just nu men notera också att handeln i USA är stängd idag pga. Thanksgiving. 
Trots den starka makrodatan under dagen (se nedan) så fortsatte amerikanska räntor att tappa och ökat intresse för säkrare statspapperen när börsen skakar verkar som en rimlig drivkraft. US-dollarn tappade också generellt något under gårdagen. Oljepriset tog ett kliv högre för fösta gången på flera dagar men på 95 dollar per fat är nivåerna fortsatt betydligt lägre än i början av november. Asien har tagit rygg på återhämtningen som skedde i slutet av börsdagen i USA och indexen är generellt upp med AI-tunga Taiwan-indexet i toppen på +2,8%. Även börsterminerna indikerar en positiv start i USA men än mer i Europa idag. 
Tullar på tapeten igen. 
Igår tillkännagav Trump en rad nya tullar mot 14 länder däribland EU, Kina, Japan och Sydkorea medan Norge klarade sig utan. Tullar på upp till 20% föreslås för specifika varugrupper där Kina och Vietnam föreslås få de högsta nivåerna medan EU förslås en nivå på 15%. De här tullarna kommer inte implementeras omedelbart utan det antyds att det kommer dröja månader innan de kan träda i kraft. 
Högre inflation och tillväxt i USA.
 Feds favoritmått på inflationen kärn-PCE överraskade igår något på uppsidan mätt i årstakt när den kom in på 3,3% mot förväntade 3,2% att jämföras med 3,1% i september. Samtidigt överraskade den andra mätningen av BNP för tredje kvartalet också på uppsidan med en kraftig uppgång om 4,3% snarare än den förväntade om 3,5% (uppräknad årstakt). Tillväxten har fortsatt främst drivits av stark konsumtion, men också av en ökning av för IT-utrustning och programvara vilket vi betraktar som ett mått på AI-investeringar. Det finns därför fog för viss oro framöver om AI-frossan håller i sig och båda dessa tillväxtdrivande komponenter får sig lite av en törn. Den lite högre inflationssiffran tillsammans med starkare tillväxt stärker caset för att Fed höjer räntan i december och att de signalerar en eller fler höjningar i deras prognoser för 2027. Notera att vi igår, redan innan datan, la till en höjning i mars till våra prognoser – mer 
här
. 
Dagens agenda är relativt tunn
 där USA är stängt för Thanksgiving. Vi har att se fram emot tyskt konsumentförtroende, norsk BNP för tredje kvartalet, Riksgäldens rapport om upplåningen (mer nedan), ett tal från Riksbankens Jansson (Svensk penningpolitik i en osäker omvärld) och så börjar ett två dagars Euro summit idag. 
Norsk BNP för tredje kvartalet idag och budget igår.
 BNP i fastlandsekonomien ökade med 0,3% under andra kvartalet, medan tillväxten under första kvartalet reviderades marginellt nedåt. Det tyder på lägre årlig tillväxt i år än vad som tidigare förväntades. Vi, konsensus och Norges Bank är dock eniga om att även tredje kvartalet kommer att visa en ökning på 0,3% där data från produktionssidan i stort sett är neutrala medan det är mer blandat på efterfrågesidan. Efter intensiva förhandlingar presenterades ett reviderat statsbudgetförslag för 2027 igår men då Miljöpartier valde att stå utanför uppgörelsen är det inte säkert att budgeten kommer få majoritetsstöd i parlamentet.  
Sverige
Riksgälden rapporterar om upplåning idag kl. 09:30.
 Vi tror att Riksgälden minskar utbudet av nominella obligationsemissioner något under 2027 jämfört med planerna från maj och att antalet veckovisa auktioner minskar från 48 till 45, vilket innebär en total på 225 miljarder under 2027. De kommer att invänta en formell begäran från Riksbanken innan man inkluderar en ökad emission av valutaobligationer i prognosen, men kommer sannolikt redan nu att diskutera möjliga konsekvenser i rapporten. Läs mer i 
360 Sweden
. 
Svenska producentpriser steg i oktober.
 Producentprisindex, som publicerades för oktober igår, steg med 0,9%. Det var något överraskande då vi snarare trott på en nedgång om 0,2%. Uppgången kom dels då elpriserna fortsatt upp istället för att som vi tänkt tillfälligt sjunka. Därtill steg priserna på exportvaror och konsumtionsvaror något och vi ser även att ett visst uppåttrycket från växelkursen troligen också bidrog. Angående elpriserna noterar vi återigen kraftiga uppgångar inför helgen och november som helhet kommer stark bidra uppåt på kommande PPI.

articles.title: Snap election in Spain – a solution to the parliamentary deadlock?
articles.heading: Euro area outlook
articles.fulltext:
Spain will hold a snap election on 29 November following a prolonged period of parliamentary deadlock. Opinion polls point to a change of government. The next government will inherit a relatively favourable economic backdrop, with strong growth and a declining public debt-to-GDP ratio. The main risk is continued political uncertainty and difficulties in passing budgets and reforms, rather than an immediate deterioration in public finances.
Key points
Snap election to break parliamentary deadlock
Strong economy provides a favourable starting point
A stable and reform-oriented Spanish government could help contain risk premia
Snap election following parliamentary deadlock
In early October, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election for 29 November after the government’s proposals to address the housing crisis were voted down. The proposals included stronger protection against evictions and extensions of expiring rental contracts. The housing crisis has triggered widespread protests across Spain. However, the underlying reason for calling the election was the parliamentary deadlock. Sánchez’s government – comprising the Socialist Party (PSOE) and the left-wing alliance Sumar, which has been reconstituted as Frente Amplio ahead of the election – lacks a stable parliamentary majority. The government has relied on support from smaller regional parties, including Catalan separatists and Basque nationalists. The fragmented parliament has made it particularly difficult to pass new budgets. Spain has not adopted a new budget since 2023. The aim of the snap election is therefore to secure stronger parliamentary support. The next scheduled general election was due to take place in 2027.
A shift to the right?
Opinion polls show a relatively tight race between the two largest parties, the conservative Partido Popular (PP) and the centre-left social democratic party PSOE, with PP holding a slight lead. Together with the national-conservative Vox, however, PP appears to be in a position to secure a parliamentary majority, provided the two parties can reach an agreement on governing together.
PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo is currently seen as the favourite to become Spain’s next prime minister. However, Sánchez has a track record of strong electoral performances despite political headwinds, and the possibility of him remaining in office cannot be ruled out. Increased fragmentation among smaller left-wing parties could, however, make it particularly difficult for Sánchez to secure sufficient parliamentary support to govern. A defeat for PSOE would mark a historic turning point, given that the party has governed Spain for almost 30 years across three separate periods since the restoration of democracy following the death of dictator Francisco Franco in 1975.
The election campaign has been dominated by the housing crisis, corruption scandals surrounding PSOE, the handling of migrants in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, and high but varying levels of regional debt and borrowing requirements. Railway safety has also come into focus following two major train accidents that claimed more than 100 lives. A victory for the right would mark the end of eight years of Sánchez and socialist-led governments.
Strong economy provides a tailwind for the next government
Spain has enjoyed strong growth since the post-pandemic recovery. Several factors explain this performance: a robust services sector supported by tourism, immigration, increased investment financed by the EU’s recovery fund, and a more favourable energy mix that has enabled Spain to weather recent energy crises better than countries such as Germany. The next government will thus inherit a relatively favourable economic starting point, with a high but declining public debt-to-GDP ratio.
Implications for fiscal policy
The fragmented parliament has meant that Spain has not adopted a new budget since 2023. A functioning PP-led majority government, supported by Vox, could reduce uncertainty and facilitate the budget process, while a persistently fragmented parliament risks delaying reforms and budget decisions. Public debt stood at just over 100% of GDP in 2025 but is expected by the European Commission to fall below this level this year. Meanwhile, the budget deficit is projected to widen slightly to just over 2.5% of GDP in 2026 before narrowing to 2.2% in 2027.
France’s strained fiscal position has drawn attention to other highly indebted countries, including Spain. Spanish sovereign bond spreads over Germany have also widened somewhat, but considerably less than their French counterparts. In our view, developments in France and broader risks surrounding European public finances are more important drivers of Spanish government bonds than the election outcome itself. However, a stable and reform-oriented Spanish government could help contain risk premia.
PP’s election manifesto includes tax cuts, a more restrictive immigration policy and a less ambitious climate policy. A stable PP-led government could reduce political uncertainty, facilitate reforms and improve the prospects for continued fiscal consolidation. However, the scope for consolidation will depend on the specific policy measures implemented. Proposed tax cuts and higher defence spending, for example, could make it more difficult to reduce the budget deficit.
The risks associated with the snap election primarily concern the ability to form a government capable of making decisions and implementing its policies. Strong economic growth should facilitate fiscal consolidation. However, successful consolidation requires a government with sufficient parliamentary support to pass new budgets. Rolling over previous budgets is not a sustainable long-term solution if Spain is to reduce its high level of public debt.

articles.title: Large SEK selling need in November
articles.heading: Rebalancing flows
articles.fulltext:
Our model estimates that typical Swedish portfolio managers have relatively large SEK selling requirements in their monthly currency rebalancing this November. The most pronounced flow is USD buying vs SEK selling. The stylised portfolio lost 1.1% in November, bringing its year-to-date return down to 3.4%.
SEK selling requirements
This November, rebalancing implies a historically relatively large SEK selling need of -0.6% of the portfolio and a USD buying need of 0.5% of the portfolio.
Large need to buy USD/SEK in November
Historical outcomes of SEK rebalancing needs
Source: SEB
Portfolio implications 
Currency hedge:
The stylised portfolio used in our analysis lost 1.1% in November, which implies only a small need to rebalance the hedge ratios (corresponding to -0.1% of the portfolio).
Bonds & Equity: 
Relative monthly performance points to a small need to buy Swedish equities (corresponding to 0.04% of the portfolio) and a need to sell Swedish bonds (corresponding to -0.52% of the portfolio). Together, the allocation rebalancing implies net SEK selling of -0.48% of the portfolio.
Market developments November
All in all:
 Combining the hedge and allocation rebalancing needs results in total SEK selling of -0.58% of the portfolio in November.

articles.title: Continued rate hikes amid a tug-of-war between inflation and AI equity concerns
articles.heading: Fed policy outlook
articles.fulltext:
Hawkish comments from several Fed officials suggest that the Fed will raise rates again in December and that policymakers will project at least one further hike in 2027. We now expect the Fed to hike twice more, in December this year and in March next year, although developments in the Middle East, inflation, AI and financial markets will be key. Fed Chair Warsh has embarked on a reform agenda at the Fed, but at least as far as communication policy is concerned, he does not appear to have the rest of the Fed on board.
Key points
Fed to raise rates and rate projections in December
We revise our Fed forecast to include another hike in March
Fed officials push back against Warsh’s communication strategy
After raising its policy rate in September – for the first time in just over three years – the US Federal Reserve left rates unchanged at 3.75–4.00% at its 27–28 October meeting. According to the minutes of the October meeting, however, almost all participants expected further monetary tightening in the months ahead, broadly in line with the projections presented at the September meeting. In September, a majority of Fed participants (10 out of 18) signalled that one additional hike in 2026 would be sufficient, but almost as many (eight participants) expected the Fed to raise rates at least once more in 2027. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh wants Fed officials to stop publishing projections and once again refrained from submitting his own projections.
High CPI inflation could prompt Waller to vote for a 50bp hike
Since the October meeting, data have pointed to a continued surprisingly resilient economy. Employment growth was stronger than expected in October, household demand remained robust and inflationary pressures were unexpectedly strong and fairly broad-based, according to the October CPI report. Meanwhile, signals from Fed officials have become increasingly hawkish. Some officials, most notably Christopher Waller, have even begun discussing a 50bp hike in December, a view shared by at least one other participant, according to the October minutes. The majority, however, appear to favour a more cautious approach, with smaller but more frequent rate hikes, either at every meeting or every other meeting. Most Fed officials have said that rates need to rise further, and some, though not all, have referred to rate hikes in the plural. New York Fed President and FOMC Vice Chair John Williams recently said that he supported further tightening but saw no need for “dramatic” action, a clear signal that he does not favour 50bp hikes. He does not, however, exclude moving at consecutive meetings, if needed. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson has also struck a more balanced tone in his speeches.
Fed divided over the rationale for raising rates
We still see the Fed as divided between those who see an immediate need for tightening to prevent inflation from accelerating further and those who view rate hikes as a precautionary measure but do not actually wish to restrain growth. The further acceleration in inflation following the rise in energy prices is a concern for Fed officials, given the risk that more than five years of above-target inflation could start to affect both corporate pricing behaviour and wage-setting. Fed officials have also begun placing greater emphasis on the inflationary risks associated with the AI build-out, which, at least initially, is seen as an upside risk to both growth and inflation. However, most participants, at least in October, viewed the inflationary pressures stemming from tariffs, energy prices and the AI build-out as temporary and expected inflation to return to target over time. Market-implied inflation expectations have declined, driven by falling fuel prices, while household inflation expectations have remained stable. Lower energy prices do not appear to have affected the tone of Fed communication but should help alleviate concerns, provided energy prices continue to decline in line with futures prices.
Equity market turmoil tightens financial conditions
Another reason to proceed cautiously is the recent equity market turmoil. Like many other observers, the Fed believes that rising equity prices have helped sustain household consumption. In October, participants assessed financial conditions as supportive, partly reflecting elevated equity valuations. If AI stocks continue to fall, putting further downward pressure on broader equity markets, the Fed may no longer regard financial conditions as equally supportive. At the same time, the Fed’s own rate hikes appear to have contributed to equity market jitters. The decline in AI stocks can partly be attributed to a less favourable political landscape in the US, with pledges from Democrats at state level to slow the pace of the AI build-out and (likely empty) threats from President Trump to impose punitive taxes on companies building data centres abroad. However, we also believe that the decline reflects the renewed rise in long-term interest rates, which both increases borrowing costs for AI companies and raises the discount rate applied to their earnings. During November, the 10-year US Treasury yield has occasionally traded above 5% again and, as before, the increase has been driven by rising real yields rather than higher break-even inflation rates.
The unexpectedly high October CPI reading and Waller’s comments about 50bp hikes prompted rates markets to raise their expectations of Fed tightening, at one point pricing in more than three additional hikes. Following the equity market decline, expectations were scaled back again. At the time of writing, rates markets are pricing in just over 2½ hikes by next summer.
Fed to raise rates and rate projections in December
At the December meeting, Fed officials will both decide on the policy rate and present updated projections for the economy and interest rates. We expect the Fed to raise rates to 4.00–4.25%, with unanimous support for further tightening (although we cannot rule out Waller and possibly another member voting in favour of a 50bp hike). At the same time, we expect the median rate projection to shift towards one additional hike next year.
We revise our Fed forecast to include another hike in March
For some time, we have forecasted a Fed rate hike in December, followed by unchanged rates. However, the higher-than-expected October CPI reading, combined with hawkish Fed comments and persistent upside risks to inflation, now leads us to expect another hike in March next year. Persistently elevated energy prices have increased the risk of spillover effects on other prices, for example through higher transport costs. Indicators such as producer prices for consumer goods and services point to continued upward pressure on consumer price inflation in the near term, and we have revised our core inflation forecasts for both this year and next year slightly higher. Lower oil prices over the past month have somewhat reduced the risk of indirect effects, however.
Our revised forecast implies that the policy rate will peak at 4.25–4.50%. This is above Fed officials’ estimates of the longer-run neutral rate. Estimates of the neutral rate vary considerably among Fed officials, but all September projections fell within a range of 2.9–3.9%, with a median of 3.2%. We expect the Fed to cut rates towards the end of 2027 and three more times in 2028, bringing the policy rate to 3.25–3.50% by the end of 2028. The endpoint is unchanged from our previous forecast.
Risks on both the upside and downside
Developments in the Middle East conflict and their impact on energy prices, inflation data over the coming months, the strength of the AI build-out and developments in financial markets will all be key to assessing the monetary policy outlook. We see risks to our forecast in both directions.
The Fed’s preferred inflation measure, core PCE, has been above core CPI since late last year, contrary to the historical pattern. We expect the two measures to converge again, with core PCE inflation peaking slightly above 3% at the end of this year before gradually approaching the 2% target again by the end of 2028.
As regards the war with Iran, President Trump continues to send mixed signals about renewed attacks. Meanwhile, the blockade of Iran has put the country in a difficult position, prompting Iran to attack US targets in the region in an attempt to pressure the US into accepting Iran’s terms for ending the war. Should hostilities intensify, the risk of an even more prolonged period of elevated energy prices would increase, adding further upward pressure on US inflation. Continued equity market turmoil, on the other hand, could prompt the Fed to proceed more cautiously, partly to avoid exacerbating the situation at a time when deteriorating financing conditions for AI companies could threaten growth, both directly through a smaller contribution from the AI build-out and indirectly through negative wealth effects on consumption.
Fed officials push back against Warsh’s communication strategy
Fed Chair Warsh has established five task forces tasked with improving the Fed’s monetary policy analysis and practices in the areas of communication, balance sheet policy, economic data, productivity and labour markets, and inflation. The intention was for the task forces to complete their work towards the end of the year. We may therefore gain some new insights from Warsh at the December press conference. One issue that has come into focus is the Fed’s communication policy, with Warsh seeking both to abandon forward guidance on upcoming policy decisions and to stop publishing individual economic and interest rate projections.
Recent communication from other Fed officials suggests that Warsh has struggled to bring his colleagues on board. While Warsh has been cautious about elaborating on his views regarding the future path of interest rates, comments and speeches from other Fed officials have, if anything, become more frequent. Several officials also appear to argue that the less the Fed says about interest rates, the faster and more aggressively it may be forced to tighten, as it would no longer be able to rely on financial markets to do some of the work for it. Several officials have also explicitly stated that they see benefits in continuing to publish individual projections. It will therefore be interesting to hear what Warsh has to say on this issue in December, as well as whether he intends to maintain the practice of holding a press conference after every meeting in the years ahead.

articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
Trots 
presidentstöd och stående ovationer

Nasdaq föll 1,5 procent medan Dow Jones gick mot strömmen och steg 0,9 procent – möjligen ett tecken på rotation från rena AI-bolag till den bredare industrisektorn. Amerikansk inflation väntas stiga.
 En av veckans viktigaste hållpunkter är amerikansk PCE-inflation för oktober, den sista inflationssiffran före Feds räntebesked den 9 december. Prognosen är att kärn-PCE, som är Feds föredragna inflationsmått, stiger 0,3 procent i månadstakt för tredje månaden i rad, vilket också skulle innebära att årstakten tickar upp med två tiondelar till 3,3 procent. Fed får därmed ytterligare en viktig pusselbit inför decembermötet i ett läge där både tillväxt- och inflationssignalerna varit starkare än väntat.

AI-driven tillväxt. 
Inflationen publiceras samtidigt som den andra beräkningen av amerikansk BNP för tredje kvartalet. Den första uppskattningen visade en tillväxt på 3,4 procent i uppräknad årstakt, där både investeringar och hushållskonsumtion bidrog starkt. AI-relaterade investeringar är en mycket viktig drivkraft bakom tillväxten i USA. Utöver inflation och BNP publiceras även statistik över bland annat inkomster, konsumtion och orderingången för varaktiga varor, och under kvällen släpper Fed sin Beige Book.

Svenska producentpriser.
 På hemmaplan publiceras producentprisindex för oktober. Vi räknar med att PPI sjunker 0,2 procent jämfört med föregående månad, främst till följd av tillfälligt lägre elpriser. Samtidigt väntas en något svagare krona ge ett visst uppåttryck på producentpriserna för konsumentvaror. Trots högre energipriser bedömer vi att det fortfarande finns få tecken på bredare indirekta effekter via internationella producentpriser.
